s: Roy is Professor Presbury's faithful wolf-hound. He attacks Presbury on several occasions while attacking no one else, is eventually banished to the stables and chained near them, and barks furiously when Presbury appears at Edith's window.

s: The Presbury case concerns unexplained changes in Professor Presbury's behavior, secret communications, a guarded box, Roy's attacks, nocturnal crawling, and Edith's sighting of Presbury at her window. Holmes considers the case obscure but believes its incidents may be linked to particular dates.

l: Professor Presbury's transformation and strange behavior, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE CREEPING MAN
s: After returning from his journey, Professor Presbury becomes furtive and sly, behaves in a sinister and unexpected manner, and sometimes appears not to remember what he has done. He is seen crawling through the passage on his hands and feet, becomes fierce toward Edith, and is seen at her second-floor window despite the lack of any apparent means of reaching it.

l: Professor Presbury's visit to Prague, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE CREEPING MAN
s: Professor Presbury leaves home without saying where he is going, remains away for a fortnight, and returns travel-worn without explaining his destination. A letter from a fellow-student in Prague reveals that Presbury had been seen there.

l: Roy's attacks on Professor Presbury, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE CREEPING MAN
s: Roy attacks Professor Presbury on July 2, July 11, and July 20. Since Roy attacks no one else, the incidents are treated as a significant part of the mystery, and Roy is later removed to the stables.

l: Professor Presbury's nocturnal crawling, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE CREEPING MAN
s: On September 4, Trevor Bennett sees Professor Presbury crawling along the dark passage at about two in the morning. Presbury moves on his hands and feet, suddenly stands upright when Bennett speaks to him, spits out an atrocious word, and leaves the house until daylight.

l: Edith's sighting of her father's face at the window, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE CREEPING MAN
s: On the night before Edith comes to Baker Street, she sees Professor Presbury's face pressed against the window of her second-floor room. She sees no ladder or other possible means of access, and Presbury makes no reference to the incident the next morning.

l: the letters from London, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE CREEPING MAN
s: Professor Presbury tells Trevor Bennett that letters from London marked with a cross under the stamp are to be reserved for him. Several arrive bearing the E.C. mark in illiterate handwriting, and any replies do not pass through Bennett or the household letter-basket.

l: the wooden box (Professor Presbury's box), The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE CREEPING MAN
s: Professor Presbury brings a small carved wooden box back from his travels and places it in his instrument cupboard. When Trevor Bennett accidentally handles it while looking for a cannula, Presbury reacts with unusual anger and savagery.

l: Baker Street, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE CREEPING MAN
s: Sherlock Holmes receives Dr. Watson and Trevor Bennett at Baker Street, where they discuss Professor Presbury's conduct and the recent incidents. Edith Presbury later comes there to seek Holmes's help.

l: Camford, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE CREEPING MAN
s: Camford is where Professor Presbury lives and works as a famous physiologist. Holmes plans to travel there with Dr. Watson and stay at the Chequers while beginning the investigation.

l: the Professor's engagement to Alice Morphy, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE CREEPING MAN
s: Professor Presbury becomes engaged to Alice Morphy, the daughter of his colleague Professor Morphy, despite being sixty-one and much older than her. His family considers the relationship excessive, while Alice's father does not object, and Holmes notes that the engagement preceded Presbury's journey and later behavioral changes.

s: Holmes and Watson visit Professor Presbury at his Camford home, pretending they were summoned, but Presbury angrily denies having contacted Holmes and drives them out. Mr. Bennett apologizes and explains that Presbury is becoming more sinister, while Holmes learns that Presbury corresponds with a London man named Dorak and that Miss Presbury remains in danger. Holmes sends Mercer to investigate Dorak and theorizes that Presbury takes a poisonous drug every nine days, a habit learned in Prague. Holmes expects a crisis the following Tuesday and plans to return to Camford.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Monday morning found us on our way to the famous University town--an
s: Holmes visits Professor Presbury in Camford with Watson, claiming that he was summoned, in order to establish personal contact. l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Monday morning found us on our way to the famous University town--an
s: Watson accompanies Holmes to Camford and observes Presbury's appearance, violent behavior, and apparent pursuit of them. He questions how the angry wolf-hound, the Prague visit, the crawling man, and the dates might be connected.

l: Professor Presbury, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Monday morning found us on our way to the famous University town--an
s: Professor Presbury receives Holmes and Watson but denies summoning Holmes and becomes intensely angry when they cannot prove their claim. He blocks their exit, rages incoherently, and later returns to the house with Mr. Bennett in an animated conversation, although his mind appears clear.

l: Mr. Bennett, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Monday morning found us on our way to the famous University town--an
s: Mr. Bennett confirms that he handles Professor Presbury's correspondence and has no record of a note sent to Holmes. He apologizes for Presbury's conduct, says that Presbury is becoming more sinister while remaining mentally clear, gives Holmes Dorak's address from blotting-paper, and warns that Presbury's daughter and he are alarmed.

l: Edith Presbury, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Monday morning found us on our way to the famous University town--an
s: Miss Presbury is regarded by Mr. Bennett as being in danger from her father. Holmes advises that she prolong her visit away from home until the danger has passed.

s: Dorak is the London man to whom Professor Presbury writes. Mercer reports that Dorak is an elderly, suave Bohemian who keeps a large general store.

l: Camford, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Monday morning found us on our way to the famous University town--an
s: Camford is the famous university town where Professor Presbury lives and lectures. Holmes and Watson visit it, plan to return the following Tuesday, and stay at an ancient hotel there.

s: Holmes investigates Professor Presbury's unexplained behavior, including violent episodes, the angry wolf-hound, a face at a window, and a man crawling down a passage. l: the Professor's drug-related outbursts, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Monday morning found us on our way to the famous University town--an
s: Holmes theorizes that Professor Presbury's violent outbursts are intensified by a poisonous drug. He notes episodes on July 2, August 26, and September 3, with the later incidents falling into a nine-day sequence.

l: the strong drug, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Monday morning found us on our way to the famous University town--an
s: Holmes provisionally identifies the strong drug as a substance that produces a temporary but highly poisonous effect and intensifies Presbury's naturally violent nature. He believes Presbury learned to use it in Prague and receives it through a Bohemian intermediary in London.

l: the Professor's correspondence with Dorak, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, Monday morning found us on our way to the famous University town--an
s: Professor Presbury secretly corresponds with Dorak in London. Mr. Bennett obtains Dorak's address from Presbury's blotting-paper after seeing that Presbury appears to have written to him that morning.

s: Holmes observes that trouble began on July 2 and then generally recurred at nine-day intervals, including August 26 and September 3. He considers the pattern too exact to be coincidence and expects new developments by the following Tuesday.

Holmes and the others discover letters, a syringe, and serum bottles showing that Presbury has been receiving a treatment from H. Lowenstein of Prague involving black-faced Langur serum. Holmes concludes that the treatment was intended to rejuvenate Presbury but caused him to revert to animal behavior, and he plans to hold Lowenstein responsible.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Mr. Bennett slipped round to bring us the latest report.
s: Sherlock Holmes identifies the significance of Professor Presbury's nine-day symptoms, his changed knuckles, the dog, and the ivy. He witnesses Presbury's animal-like behavior, investigates the locked box, reads H. Lowenstein's letter, and concludes that Langur serum caused the transformation. He plans to write to Lowenstein and hold him criminally responsible for distributing the poisons.

l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Mr. Bennett slipped round to bring us the latest report.
s: Dr. Watson joins Sherlock Holmes in observing Professor Presbury's house and the Professor's nocturnal behavior. He helps separate Roy from Presbury, dresses the Professor's torn throat, gives him morphia, and records the investigation.

l: Professor Presbury, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Mr. Bennett slipped round to bring us the latest report.
s: Professor Presbury appears normal during the day but at the expected ninth-day crisis leaves his house in a crouch, crawls on his hands and feet, climbs the ivy with unusual agility, and provokes the wolf-hound. Roy attacks him and tears his throat, leaving him seriously wounded and unconscious. His box contains serum bottles, a hypodermic syringe, and correspondence revealing that he has been receiving a Langur-based treatment from H. Lowenstein.

l: Mr. Bennett, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Mr. Bennett slipped round to bring us the latest report.
s: Mr. Bennett reports on Professor Presbury's behavior and helps Holmes and Dr. Watson keep the Professor under observation. He follows Presbury from the house, helps rescue him after Roy's attack, dresses his wound, and provides the key to the Professor's box.

l: H. Lowenstein, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Mr. Bennett slipped round to bring us the latest report.
s: H. Lowenstein writes from Prague to Professor Presbury about the treatment and warns that it may be dangerous. l: Roy, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Mr. Bennett slipped round to bring us the latest report.
s: Roy is the wolf-hound kept at the Professor's stables. He recognizes and violently reacts to Presbury's transformed behavior; after Presbury deliberately torments him, his collar slips and he attacks Presbury, biting deeply into his throat.

l: Prague, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Mr. Bennett slipped round to bring us the latest report.
s: Prague is identified as the place Professor Presbury visited before his symptoms began and as the location from which H. Lowenstein sends correspondence about the treatment. Holmes considers the connection between Prague and the serum central to the case.

l: the Serum of Anthropoid, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Mr. Bennett slipped round to bring us the latest report.
s: The Serum of Anthropoid is mentioned by H. Lowenstein as a possible treatment that might have been better suited to Professor Presbury's case. Lowenstein used black-faced Langur instead because that specimen was accessible.

l: black-faced Langur, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Mr. Bennett slipped round to bring us the latest report.
s: Black-faced Langur is the animal source Lowenstein used for Professor Presbury's serum because a specimen was available. Lowenstein describes Langur as a crawler and climber, unlike the more erect-walking Anthropoid.

l: the treatment, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Mr. Bennett slipped round to bring us the latest report.
s: The treatment given to Professor Presbury involves serum administered by hypodermic syringe according to directions regulating a nine-day cycle. It produces increased energy and vitality but also causes Presbury to display crawling, climbing, and other animal-like behavior, and Lowenstein warns that it is dangerous.

l: rejuvenescence, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Mr. Bennett slipped round to bring us the latest report.
s: Rejuvenescence is associated with Lowenstein's reported scientific efforts to discover a means of restoring youth. Holmes concludes that Professor Presbury pursued the treatment because he wanted to become a younger man.

l: the wolf-hound attack, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Mr. Bennett slipped round to bring us the latest report.
s: The wolf-hound attack occurs after Professor Presbury deliberately provokes Roy with pebbles, a stick, and gestures near the dog's mouth. Roy's collar slips, allowing him to seize Presbury by the throat and cause serious bleeding before Holmes, Dr. Watson, Bennett, and the coachman intervene.

l: Professor Presbury's visit to Prague, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Mr. Bennett slipped round to bring us the latest report.
s: Professor Presbury's visit to Prague precedes the beginning of his strange symptoms. Holmes connects the visit with Presbury's secret correspondence with a Bohemian dealer in London and with H. Lowenstein's serum treatment.

l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
s: After retiring to Sussex, Mr. Holmes investigates the death of Fitzroy McPherson, who is found dying near the beach after suffering terrible unexplained injuries. McPherson’s last words appear to identify the “Lion’s Mane,” while his body bears long, curved red weals resembling scourge marks. Suspicion falls partly on Ian Murdoch, who had visited The Haven, was dismissed by Harold Stackhurst, and may have had feelings for Maud Bellamy. Holmes and Stackhurst learn that McPherson and Maud were secretly engaged and begin examining the possible motives and circumstances surrounding the assault.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
s: Mr. Holmes, living in retirement near the Sussex coast, discovers Fitzroy McPherson dying and takes charge of the initial investigation. He examines the beach, the footprints, McPherson’s belongings, and the correspondence connecting McPherson with Maud Bellamy.

l: Harold Stackhurst, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
s: Harold Stackhurst encounters Mr. Holmes while going for a swim and helps him respond when Fitzroy McPherson collapses. He remains with McPherson’s body, reports on the relationships at The Gables, dismisses Ian Murdoch after their confrontation, and assists Holmes in questioning the Bellamy family.

l: Fitzroy McPherson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
s: Fitzroy McPherson, the science master at The Gables, is found staggering up from the beach and dies after suffering severe unexplained pain. He had prepared to swim but apparently never entered the water, and he was secretly engaged to Maud Bellamy.

l: Ian Murdoch, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
s: Ian Murdoch, the mathematical coach at The Gables, arrives after McPherson collapses and denies being with him on the beach. He had held the students back with an algebra demonstration, had visited The Haven, and is dismissed by Stackhurst after an angry exchange.

l: Maud Bellamy, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
s: Maud Bellamy is the daughter of Tom Bellamy and is described as exceptionally beautiful and strong-minded. She confirms that she and McPherson were engaged, offers Holmes her help, and says that more than one person may have been needed to inflict his injuries.

l: Fulworth, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
s: Fulworth is the nearby village around the bay, containing the police station and the Bellamy family’s home and boating business. Holmes and Stackhurst walk there to question the Bellamys.

l: The Gables, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
s: The Gables is Harold Stackhurst’s coaching establishment, where young men prepare for professions and where Stackhurst, McPherson, and Murdoch work. McPherson’s body is taken there, and Stackhurst later dismisses Murdoch from the establishment.

l: The Haven, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
s: The Haven is the Bellamy family home in Fulworth. Ian Murdoch is seen leaving it when Holmes and Stackhurst arrive to speak with the Bellamys.

l: the beach, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
s: The beach lies below the chalk cliffs and includes a lagoon, swimming-pools, caves, pebbles, and shingle. McPherson went there intending to bathe, but the beach appeared deserted apart from distant figures, and his footprints and towel were found there.

l: the chalk cliffs, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
s: The coast near Holmes’s villa consists of chalk cliffs that can be descended by a single steep, slippery path. Small caves at their base are searched after McPherson’s death, but nothing is found.

l: Fitzroy McPherson's death, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
s: Fitzroy McPherson’s death occurs after he staggers up from the beach, cries out about the Lion’s Mane, and collapses. His death is treated as an extraordinary and apparently criminal event because his body shows signs of intense suffering and violent injury.

l: the assault on Fitzroy McPherson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
s: The assault leaves McPherson’s back covered with dark red, curved lines like marks from a thin wire scourge. He appears to have been tortured until he bit through his lower lip, then managed only to crawl away from the beach before dying.

l: the Lion's Mane mystery, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
s: The Lion’s Mane mystery begins when McPherson’s final warning appears to be the words “the lion’s mane.” The phrase is initially unintelligible to Holmes and becomes the name of the unusual problem he begins investigating.

l: the investigation, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
s: The investigation examines McPherson’s movements, footprints, clothing, towel, body, personal papers, and relationships. Holmes and Stackhurst question the Bellamys and begin to focus on Ian Murdoch, Maud Bellamy, and the possibility of multiple attackers.

l: the McPherson–Bellamy engagement, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
s: McPherson and Maud Bellamy were secretly engaged to be married. They kept the engagement secret because McPherson’s elderly uncle might have disinherited him if he married against his uncle’s wishes.

l: the note from Maud Bellamy, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
s: A note in McPherson’s card-case, written in a feminine hand, reads, “I will be there, you may be sure.--Maudie.” The note suggests an assignation, and McPherson’s papers identify Maud Bellamy as its writer.

l: the scourge, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
s: The apparent scourge is the suspected instrument that produced the long, flexible-looking weals on McPherson’s back. No actual scourge is found, and Holmes questions whether a human hand wielded it.

l: McPherson's body, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
s: McPherson’s body is found on the path above the beach, with his Burberry thrown around his shoulders, disordered clothing, blood on his chin, and severe red marks across his back. His pockets contain a handkerchief, a large knife, a folding card-case, and the note signed “Maudie.”

l: Murdoch's possible motive, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE LION'S MANE
s: Murdoch’s possible motive includes his former apparent interest in Maud Bellamy, his earlier hostility toward McPherson, and his visit to The Haven shortly after McPherson’s death. Holmes also notes that Murdoch had an angry temperament and appeared to be seeking a way to leave the scene.

s: Sherlock Holmes connects the deaths of Fitzroy McPherson and McPherson's dog, along with Ian Murdoch's sudden illness, to a deadly jellyfish in the bathing-pool. The phrase “Lion's Mane,” spoken by McPherson before his death, is recognized as a warning describing the creature. Cyanea capillata is crushed beneath a boulder, McPherson's death is explained as an accidental envenomation, and Ian Murdoch is exonerated.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
s: Sherlock Holmes investigates the unexplained death of Fitzroy McPherson and initially considers Ian Murdoch a possible suspect. After learning of the dog's death and recalling information from J. G. Wood's Out of Doors, he identifies Cyanea capillata in the bathing-pool and explains the deaths and attacks as jellyfish stings.

l: Fitzroy McPherson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
s: Fitzroy McPherson died at the bathing-pool with strange injuries that initially suggested a violent assault. Sherlock Holmes concludes that he was killed by the stinging filaments of Cyanea capillata, and that his final words, “Lion's Mane,” warned of the creature.

l: Ian Murdoch, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
s: Ian Murdoch is suspected of killing Fitzroy McPherson because of his temper, his past quarrel with McPherson, and his feelings for Miss Bellamy. He is attacked by Cyanea capillata at the same beach and survives after suffering severe pain, thereby clearing himself of suspicion.

l: Harold Stackhurst, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
s: Stackhurst investigates the disappearance and death of Fitzroy McPherson and brings Ian Murdoch to Sherlock Holmes after finding him stricken on the beach. He helps Holmes crush Cyanea capillata beneath a boulder and later reconciles with Murdoch.

l: Inspector Bardie, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had

l: The Gables, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
s: The Gables is where Stackhurst's students Sudbury and Blount report finding McPherson's dog and where Stackhurst is initially found in his study. Stackhurst later leaves The Gables to bring the stricken Ian Murdoch to Sherlock Holmes.

l: the bathing-pool, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
s: The bathing-pool is the site where Fitzroy McPherson died, his dog was later found dead, and Ian Murdoch was attacked. Sherlock Holmes discovers Cyanea capillata beneath the water in its deeper section and identifies it as the source of the danger.

l: the beach, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
s: The beach is where Fitzroy McPherson met his end, where his dog's tracks were found, and where Ian Murdoch suffered his attack. Its secluded bathing-pool concealed the deadly jellyfish.

l: Fitzroy McPherson's death, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
s: Fitzroy McPherson's death is initially treated as a possible murder because of the severe, patterned injuries on his body. Sherlock Holmes determines that the injuries and his last words are consistent with an attack by Cyanea capillata rather than a human assault.

l: the dog's death, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
s: The dog's death is first attributed to grief for its master after it refuses food for a week. l: Ian Murdoch's attack, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
s: Ian Murdoch's attack occurs at the edge of the water where Fitzroy McPherson died. The attack produces severe pain, breathing difficulties, and a reticulated red pattern on his shoulder, matching McPherson's injuries and revealing the true cause of the earlier death.

l: the dog (McPherson's dog), The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
s: McPherson's dog, an Airedale terrier, follows the trail of its dead master to the bathing-pool and dies at the edge of it. Its rigid, contorted body and the location of its death provide Sherlock Holmes with an important clue to the danger in the water.

l: Cyanea capillata, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
s: Cyanea capillata is a jellyfish resembling a tangled mass of tawny and silver lion's mane. It radiates nearly invisible filaments over a wide area, causing red, dotted marks, extreme pain, cardiac distress, and potentially death; Sherlock Holmes and Stackhurst crush it beneath a boulder.

l: the murder investigation, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
s: The murder investigation initially focuses on Ian Murdoch because of his relationship with Miss Bellamy, his history with McPherson, and his apparent preparations to leave. l: the reticulated sting pattern, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had
s: The reticulated sting pattern consists of criss-crossed red, inflamed lines with uneven intensity and distinct dots of extravasated blood. Sherlock Holmes sees the same pattern on Fitzroy McPherson and Ian Murdoch and recognizes it as the mark left by the jellyfish's filaments.

l: the Lion's Mane warning, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, A week passed. The inquest had thrown no light upon the matter and had

l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER

l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes to Mrs. Ronder's room and listens to Eugenia Ronder's account. He recalls the Abbas Parva case only after Holmes describes it and proposes an explanation for the positions of Ronder, Eugenia, and the lion.

l: Mrs. Merrilow, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
s: Mrs. Merrilow has rented a private room to Eugenia Ronder for seven years and has seen her face only once. She tells Sherlock Holmes that Eugenia cries out about murder and asks him to come, while chiefly fearing that anything he does might cause her valuable lodger to leave.

l: Eugenia Ronder, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
s: Eugenia Ronder, formerly Mrs. Ronder, has lived veiled and isolated for seven years because Sahara King tore apart her face. She confesses that she helped Leonardo plan Ronder's killing, but concealed the truth because Leonardo's fate and her own reputation depended on her silence.

l: Ronder, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
s: Ronder was a famous but declining wild-beast showman who drank, bullied people, abused Eugenia, and treated animals cruelly. Leonardo killed him with a club designed to leave wounds resembling a lion's paw, after which the death was officially treated as misadventure.

l: Leonardo, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
s: Leonardo was the strongman in Ronder's show and Eugenia Ronder's lover. He devised the murder plan and struck Ronder with the spiked club, but lost his nerve and fled when Sahara King came out of the cage.

l: Sahara King, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
s: Sahara King was a North African lion kept by Ronder's wild beast show. After Leonardo killed Ronder, Eugenia opened the lion's cage; the animal attacked and severely mutilated her before the circus men drove it away.

l: Abbas Parva, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
s: Abbas Parva is a small Berkshire village where Ronder's caravan stopped for the night while traveling toward Wimbledon. The killings and lion attack occurred there.

l: Ronder's wild beast show, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
s: Ronder's wild beast show was once prominent but was declining because of Ronder's drinking and conduct. It included Sahara King and employed Leonardo, Griggs, and other circus workers who witnessed the aftermath of the attack.

l: Abbas Parva tragedy, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
s: The Abbas Parva tragedy involved Ronder's death and Eugenia Ronder's severe facial mutilation beside the open lion's cage. The inquest recorded the event as death from misadventure, although Sherlock Holmes and Edmunds found aspects of the evidence troubling.

l: the lion attack at Abbas Parva, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
s: The lion attack at Abbas Parva began when Eugenia opened Sahara King's cage after Leonardo struck Ronder. The lion attacked Eugenia, tore her face, and was driven away by Leonardo, Griggs, and other men.

l: Ronder's murder, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER

l: the case, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
s: The case concerns the unexplained circumstances surrounding Ronder's death and Eugenia Ronder's mutilation at Abbas Parva. Sherlock Holmes had once been unable to resolve it, but Eugenia's confession supplies the missing explanation.

l: Mrs. Ronder's mutilated face, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
s: Mrs. Ronder's mutilated face was torn by Sahara King during the attack. She survived, hid it beneath a veil, and withdrew from society, later telling Sherlock Holmes that she wished the lion had killed her.

l: the lion's cage, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
s: The lion's cage held Sahara King and was normally used for performances by Ronder and Eugenia. Eugenia opened its door after Leonardo killed Ronder, allowing the lion to escape and attack her.

l: five-clawed club, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
s: The spiked club was made by Leonardo with a leaden head and five long steel nails arranged to resemble a lion's paw. It was used to deliver the fatal blow to Ronder while concealing the murder's true cause.

l: domestic abuse, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
s: Domestic abuse dominated Eugenia Ronder's marriage to Ronder. He tied her down, lashed her with a riding-whip, deserted her for other women, and became especially violent when drunk.

l: Leonardo and Eugenia Ronder's love affair, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
s: Leonardo and Eugenia Ronder's relationship grew from his pity and assistance to a deep, passionate love affair. Their intimacy led them to conclude that Ronder could not be allowed to continue living.

l: the murder plot, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE VEILED LODGER
s: The murder plot called for Leonardo to kill Ronder with a spiked club and for Eugenia to release Sahara King so that the death would appear to have been caused by the lion. The plan failed to protect Eugenia when Leonardo fled and the lion attacked her instead.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We sat in silence for some time after the unhappy woman had told her
s: Sherlock Holmes expresses sympathy for the unnamed woman and asks about Leonardo and the five-clawed club. He tells her that her life is not her own and urges her to endure her suffering. Two days later, he shows John Watson a blue bottle of prussic acid sent to him by post.

l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We sat in silence for some time after the unhappy woman had told her
s: John Watson is present while Sherlock Holmes speaks with the unnamed woman. Two days later, he visits Holmes, examines the blue bottle, and identifies its almondy-smelling contents as prussic acid.

l: Eugenia Ronder, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We sat in silence for some time after the unhappy woman had told her
s: The unnamed woman says that Leonardo deserted her after the lion attacked her, though she could not bring herself to send him to the gallows. She reveals that the lion left her face horribly disfigured and says she may have lost the five-clawed club in a chalk-pit pool. After Holmes urges her not to take her own life, she sends him a bottle of prussic acid with a message indicating that she will follow his advice.

l: Leonardo, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We sat in silence for some time after the unhappy woman had told her
s: Leonardo deserted the unnamed woman after leaving her under the lion's claws, and she says she never saw or heard from him again. He was drowned last month while bathing near Margate.

l: five-clawed club, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We sat in silence for some time after the unhappy woman had told her
s: The five-clawed club is described as the most singular and ingenious part of the woman's story. She does not know what Leonardo did with it and suggests that it may lie in the deep green pool at the base of a chalk-pit.

l: Leonardo's drowning, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We sat in silence for some time after the unhappy woman had told her
s: Leonardo's drowning occurred last month while he was bathing near Margate. The unnamed woman learned of his death from a newspaper.

l: the case, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We sat in silence for some time after the unhappy woman had told her
s: Sherlock Holmes declares the case closed after hearing that Leonardo is dead and that the five-clawed club may have been lost in the chalk-pit pool. The unnamed woman repeats that the case is closed.

l: blue bottle, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We sat in silence for some time after the unhappy woman had told her
s: Two days after the woman's visit, Sherlock Holmes has a small blue bottle on his mantelpiece. It bears a red poison label and contains a substance with a pleasant almondy odour.

l: prussic acid, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, We sat in silence for some time after the unhappy woman had told her
s: John Watson identifies the contents of the blue bottle as prussic acid. The substance was sent to Sherlock Holmes by post.

s: The message sent with the blue bottle says, "I send you my temptation. I will follow your advice." Sherlock Holmes and John Watson infer that it was sent by the brave unnamed woman.

l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson investigate troubling events at Shoscombe Old Place after John Mason reports that Sir Robert Norberton has become obsessed with winning the Derby, estranged from Lady Beatrice Falder, and visited a haunted crypt with an unknown man. Evidence includes Lady Beatrice's unexplained change in behavior, the removal of her beloved spaniel, mummy remains in the crypt, and a charred fragment of human bone from the central heating furnace. Holmes develops two possible lines of inquiry: a quarrel involving Lady Beatrice's maid, Carrie Evans, and the possibility that Sir Robert has killed Lady Beatrice and arranged for someone to impersonate her. Holmes and Watson travel to the Green Dragon near Shoscombe Old Place disguised as fishermen to investigate further.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
s: Sherlock Holmes examines microscopic evidence in another case before hearing John Mason's concerns about Shoscombe Old Place. He theorizes that Sir Robert may have killed Lady Beatrice, concealed her body, and arranged for someone to impersonate her, then travels with Dr. Watson to investigate while posing as a fisherman.

l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
s: Dr. Watson identifies the charred fragment as the upper condyle of a human femur and provides background about Sir Robert Norberton and Shoscombe Old Place. He accompanies Sherlock Holmes to the Green Dragon to investigate the situation.

l: Sir Robert Norberton, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
s: Sir Robert Norberton is described as a dangerous, reckless rider who has staked his finances on Shoscombe Prince winning the Derby. He has stopped visiting Lady Beatrice, given away her beloved spaniel, visited the haunted crypt at night with an unknown man, and allegedly may have killed his sister to protect his financial position.

l: Lady Beatrice Falder, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
s: Lady Beatrice Falder is Sir Robert's widowed sister and the owner of Shoscombe Old Place under a life interest. She has heart trouble and dropsy, has withdrawn from the horses, remains in her room, drinks heavily, and is described as brooding and sulky after the supposed quarrel with Sir Robert.

l: John Mason, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
s: John Mason, the head trainer at Shoscombe, asks Sherlock Holmes to investigate what he believes is strange and possibly criminal conduct by Sir Robert. He reports the household changes, the nocturnal visits to the haunted crypt, the unknown man, the mummy remains, and the charred bone fragment.

l: Carrie Evans, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
s: Carrie Evans is Lady Beatrice's maid and has served her for five years. John Mason suggests that she is devoted, but leaves unclear whether her loyalty is to Lady Beatrice or to Sir Robert.

l: the unknown man in the crypt, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
s: The unknown man in the crypt meets Sir Robert there at night. When John Mason and Stephens approach him, he reacts with terror, has a yellow face, and runs away before they can identify him.

l: Shoscombe Old Place, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
s: Shoscombe Old Place is the estate at the center of the investigation, containing the Shoscombe stud and training quarters, Lady Beatrice's rooms, a cellar furnace, and access to the park and old chapel. Its household has been disrupted by the apparent estrangement between Sir Robert and Lady Beatrice and by suspicious nighttime activity.

l: the Green Dragon, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
s: The Green Dragon is an inn at Crendall kept by Josiah Barnes, three miles from Shoscombe Old Place. Sir Robert gave Lady Beatrice's spaniel to Barnes, and Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson stay there while investigating.

l: the old ruined chapel, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
s: The old ruined chapel stands in the park of Shoscombe Old Place and is of uncertain age. A crypt beneath it is associated with Sir Robert's nighttime meetings and the discovery of hidden remains.

l: the chapel crypt (Shoscombe Old Place), The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
s: The haunted crypt beneath the old ruined chapel is considered dark, damp, lonely, and frightening at night. Sir Robert visits it after midnight, an unknown man meets him there, and John Mason later finds a head and bones concealed in one corner.

l: Shoscombe Prince, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
s: Shoscombe Prince is described as the best colt in England and Sir Robert's principal hope for financial recovery. Sir Robert has secretly backed him heavily for the Derby and uses the colt's half-brother in public training spins to conceal his ability.

l: the Shoscombe spaniels, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
s: The Shoscombe spaniels are described as an exclusive and famous breed, especially prized by Lady Beatrice. Sir Robert gives away her favorite spaniel after becoming angry with it, and the dog is later kept at the Green Dragon.

l: the central heating furnace, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
s: The central heating furnace in the cellar beneath Lady Beatrice's room had been unused until Sir Robert had it restarted because he complained of the cold. A fragment of burned human bone is found among its cinders, and the furnace can be reached from outside or through a passage near Lady Beatrice's room.

l: the charred human bone fragment, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
s: The charred human bone fragment is found by Harvey while raking the central heating furnace's cinders. Dr. Watson identifies it as the upper condyle of a human femur, making it significant evidence of possible human remains being burned.

l: the ancient human remains (chapel crypt), The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
s: The mummy remains consist of a human head and a few bones found hidden beneath a board in one corner of the haunted crypt. John Mason believes they may be a thousand years old and says they were not present there before.

l: the Derby, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
s: The Derby is the race on which Sir Robert has placed his last financial hope. He must win it with Shoscombe Prince to avoid being unable to satisfy his creditors and losing his racing stables.

l: the alleged murder of Lady Beatrice, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
s: The alleged murder of Lady Beatrice is Sherlock Holmes's hypothetical explanation for the crypt visits, the furnace evidence, and the changes in the household. Holmes suggests that Sir Robert may have disposed of her body and concealed the crime until he could realize his winnings from the Derby.

l: horse racing, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
s: Horse racing dominates Sir Robert's life and finances, with Shoscombe Prince at the center of his plans. His obsession with the horses and the Derby is said to have affected his nerves and behavior.

l: gambling and debt, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
s: Sir Robert has staked everything he could raise or borrow on Shoscombe Prince and is deeply in debt to creditors. If the horse fails in the Derby, he expects to be financially ruined, with his racing stables liable to seizure.

l: the supposed quarrel between Sir Robert and Lady Beatrice, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
s: The supposed quarrel is inferred from Sir Robert's sudden withdrawal from Lady Beatrice, his giving away of her favorite spaniel, and her refusal to engage with him or the horses. Holmes considers that the dispute may concern Carrie Evans, but also recognizes that the apparent quarrel could conceal a more serious crime.

l: the personation of Lady Beatrice, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF SHOSCOMBE OLD PLACE
s: Impersonation of Lady Beatrice is proposed by Holmes as part of a hypothetical scheme following her possible murder. He suggests that Carrie Evans could help arrange for another woman to appear in Lady Beatrice's place while Sir Robert remained at the estate until after the Derby.

l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson investigate the apparent personation of Lady Beatrice at Shoscombe Old Place. Holmes uses Lady Beatrice's black spaniel to establish that the carriage occupant is a stranger and later discovers Lady Beatrice's body hidden in an ancestral coffin in the chapel crypt. Sir Robert admits that Lady Beatrice died a week earlier and that Mr. Norlett had been personating her to delay his creditors until the Derby. Shoscombe Prince wins the Derby, allowing Sir Robert to pay his creditors, while the police and coroner treat the deception leniently.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
s: Sherlock Holmes investigates the apparent illness and identity of Lady Beatrice at Shoscombe Old Place. He uses the black spaniel to show that the woman in the carriage is a stranger, finds Lady Beatrice's body in an ancestral coffin, and compels Sir Robert to explain the concealment and personation.

l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
s: Dr. Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes in observing the carriage, questioning the coachman, searching the chapel crypt, and confronting Sir Robert. He recognizes that the voice from the carriage was that of a man and witnesses Holmes's discovery of the body.

l: Sir Robert Norberton, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
s: Sir Robert owns Shoscombe Old Place and is financially dependent on Lady Beatrice while heavily indebted. After Holmes discovers Lady Beatrice's body, he admits arranging for Mr. Norlett to personate her and hiding her body in the chapel crypt until the Derby was decided.

l: Lady Beatrice Falder, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
s: Lady Beatrice was Sir Robert's sister and the source of his financial security, with an interest in the estate lasting for her lifetime. She died of what Sir Robert says was dropsy, and her body was concealed while another person appeared publicly as her.

l: Shoscombe Prince, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
s: Shoscombe Prince was Sir Robert's dark horse for the Derby, on whose success his financial recovery depended. The horse won the Derby, enabling Sir Robert to pay his creditors and retain enough money to re-establish himself.

l: John Mason, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
s: John Mason, the trainer, meets Holmes and Watson at the park gates and leads them to the chapel crypt. He knows about bones found there but leaves before Holmes examines the ancestral coffins.

l: Mr. and Mrs. Norlett, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
s: Mr. and Mrs. Norlett are brought by Sir Robert to substantiate his account. Mr. Norlett is an actor who personated Lady Beatrice, while Mrs. Norlett had been Lady Beatrice's confidential maid under her maiden name of Evans.

l: Carrie Evans, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
s: Mrs. Norlett, formerly Evans, had served for years as Lady Beatrice's confidential maid. She was involved in the arrangement that allowed her husband to appear publicly as Lady Beatrice and protested when Sir Robert decided to explain the matter.

l: Shoscombe Old Place, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
s: Shoscombe Old Place is Sir Robert's estate, where Lady Beatrice was publicly represented after her death and where the financial crisis surrounding Shoscombe Prince was centered. Its park gates and chapel crypt are the principal locations of Holmes's investigation.

l: the chapel crypt (Shoscombe Old Place), The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
s: The chapel crypt is an old, dismal burial place containing the family's coffins. Sir Robert and Mr. Norlett used it to conceal Lady Beatrice's body after removing the remains from an ancestral coffin.

l: the Derby, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
s: The Derby was the race on which Sir Robert's financial hopes depended. Shoscombe Prince won it, producing eighty thousand pounds in bets and allowing the creditors to be paid.

l: Lady Beatrice's death, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
s: Lady Beatrice died about a week before Holmes confronted Sir Robert. Sir Robert attributed her death to dropsy, but he concealed it rather than registering it immediately because he feared financial ruin.

l: the personation of Lady Beatrice, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
s: After Lady Beatrice's death, Mr. Norlett appeared as her for several weeks, mainly by riding daily in her carriage while Mrs. Norlett controlled access to her room. The black spaniel exposed the deception by reacting with fury when it encountered the disguised person.

l: the creditors, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
s: Sir Robert feared that his creditors would seize the estate, stables, and horses if Lady Beatrice's death became known. They held their action until after the Derby and were then paid in full from Sir Robert's winnings.

l: the black spaniel (Lady Beatrice's dog), The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
s: The black spaniel initially greeted the person in the carriage as though she were its mistress, but then recognized the stranger and attacked the black skirt. Sir Robert later said he had got rid of the dog after it followed him and Mr. Norlett while they were moving Lady Beatrice's body.

l: the ancestral coffin (chapel crypt), The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
s: Holmes finds an ancestral coffin standing near the vault entrance and opens it with a jemmy. It contains Lady Beatrice's body after Sir Robert and Mr. Norlett removed the ancient remains and burned them in a furnace.

l: Lady Beatrice's body, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
s: Lady Beatrice's body was first taken to an unused well-house and then moved to the chapel crypt. Sir Robert and Mr. Norlett placed it inside an ancestral coffin, where Holmes discovers it wrapped in a sheet.

l: the financial crisis surrounding Shoscombe Prince, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
s: Sir Robert faced ruin because he depended on Lady Beatrice's estate and was deeply indebted. His financial crisis centered on the prospect that creditors would seize his horses and prevent Shoscombe Prince from running, but the horse's Derby victory resolved the danger.

l: Sir Robert's concealment of the death, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning Holmes discovered that we had come without our
s: Sir Robert concealed Lady Beatrice's death for roughly three weeks so that Shoscombe Prince could run in the Derby and his bets could succeed. He arranged the public personation, hid the body in the chapel crypt, and delayed registering the death, receiving only mild censure afterward.

l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
s: Sherlock Holmes asks Dr. John Watson to investigate Josiah Amberley's claim that Mrs. Amberley and Dr. Ray Ernest disappeared together after taking money and securities from his strong-room. Watson visits The Haven in Lewisham, hears Amberley's account, and observes the neglected house, Amberley's artificial limb, and a tall, dark man who appears to follow him. Holmes identifies several overlooked details and obtains information confirming Amberley's reputation, his wealth, and Dr. Ernest's association with him and Mrs. Amberley. Although the case initially seems simple, Holmes concludes that it has developed serious complications.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
s: Sherlock Holmes receives Josiah Amberley's case through the Yard but initially considers it commonplace. He sends Dr. John Watson to The Haven because he is occupied with the case of the two Coptic Patriarchs, then analyzes Watson's report and points out important details Watson missed.

l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
s: Dr. John Watson visits The Haven in Lewisham as Sherlock Holmes's representative and interviews Josiah Amberley. He observes the house and its surroundings, records Amberley's account, notices a tall, dark man apparently following him, and reports his findings to Holmes.

l: Josiah Amberley, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
s: Josiah Amberley, a retired junior partner of Brickfall and Amberley, lives at The Haven after retiring with a fortune and marrying a younger woman. He claims that Mrs. Amberley and Dr. Ray Ernest left together with his deed-box and about seven thousand pounds' worth of cash and securities. He appears physically burdened and emotionally devastated, and is described as a miserly, harsh, and exacting husband.

l: Amberley's wife, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
s: Mrs. Amberley is Josiah Amberley's younger wife and is described as good-looking. Amberley claims that she had an intimacy with Dr. Ray Ernest, left with him, and took his deed-box containing money and securities.

l: Dr. Ray Ernest, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
s: Dr. Ray Ernest is a young, unmarried doctor who lives near Josiah Amberley and plays chess with him. He frequently visited The Haven and is suspected by Amberley of leaving with Mrs. Amberley.

l: The Adventure of the Retired Colourman, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
s: This unit introduces Sherlock Holmes's investigation of Josiah Amberley's report that his wife and Dr. Ray Ernest disappeared after a theft. It follows Dr. John Watson's visit to The Haven and Holmes's growing suspicion that the apparently simple case has a more complicated aspect.

l: The Haven, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
s: The Haven is Josiah Amberley's neglected house in Lewisham, surrounded by a high brick wall. It contains a strong-room with an iron door and shutter, as well as the rooms and passage Amberley has been painting.

l: Lewisham, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
s: Lewisham is the London district where The Haven and Josiah Amberley's home are located. Dr. John Watson travels there to investigate Amberley's story.

l: the disappearance of Mrs. Amberley and Dr. Ernest, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
s: Josiah Amberley reports that Mrs. Amberley and Dr. Ray Ernest left together after she claimed to have a headache and remained at home while Amberley went alone to the Haymarket Theatre. Their destination is unknown, and neither has sent Amberley a letter or message.

l: the theft from the strong-room, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
s: Amberley reports that about seven thousand pounds' worth of cash and securities were taken from his burglar-proof strong-room. He says Mrs. Amberley had a duplicate key and that the door and window were open when he returned from the theatre.

l: the investigation of Amberley's case, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE RETIRED COLOURMAN
s: The investigation begins when the Yard sends Amberley to Sherlock Holmes after the police receive his report. Holmes delegates the initial visit to Dr. John Watson, gathers local information by telephone and through the Yard, and learns that Amberley was reputed to be a miser and harsh husband while Dr. Ernest had connections with both Amberley and his wife.

s: Sherlock Holmes investigates Josiah Amberley's claim that his wife and Dr. Ray Ernest disappeared with securities, and tests Amberley by sending him to Little Purlington with Dr. John Watson. The telegram supposedly sent by the Vicar is revealed to be forged, allowing Holmes to search Amberley's house while he is away. Holmes, aided by Mr. Barker, Inspector MacKinnon, and the police, identifies the strong-room as the likely death-chamber and exposes Amberley's plot to murder the couple. Amberley is arrested after Holmes confronts him about the bodies and prevents him from swallowing a poison pellet.

s: Sherlock Holmes arranged for Josiah Amberley to follow the forged telegram to Little Purlington so that he could examine Amberley's house without interruption. He discovered the gas pipe leading into the sealed strong-room, identified the wall message, confronted Amberley about the bodies, and turned his findings over to Inspector MacKinnon and the police.
